World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Solar eclipse to attract thousands to 'middle of nowhere' in 2028
World.content:
Doon Doon, in Western Australia's East Kimberley region, is a small roadhouse with a dozen transient staff and known for its oversized burgers.

But in just over two years' time, it will be put on the global map as the best place to admire one of the longest eclipses this century.

The 2028 eclipse in the East Kimberley will be one of the longest this century. (Supplied: NASA)

The region, 3,000 kilometres north of Perth, will be in complete darkness for more than five minutes and is expected to attract around 25,000 extra visitors from across the world.

Doon Doon roadhouse manager Shayne Stewart said he found out about the astronomical phenomenon just after the Exmouth eclipse in 2023, when the phone started ringing with booking requests for 2028.

Shayne Stewart says the eclipse will put Doon Doon on the world map. (Supplied: Shayne Stewart)

"I've had people from America wanting to book the whole caravan park," he said.

A big event for a small place

Mr Stewart said the eclipse would shine a light on Doon Doon and the nearby Aboriginal community of Woolah.

"They have had contact from people in Japan wanting to go to the school," he said.

The exposure will bring some challenges for the small roadhouse and community, with fewer than 100 people between locals and staff welcoming thousands of visitors to "the middle of nowhere".

"I'm not so worried about the event. I'm worried about the size of it," Mr Stewart said.

But preparations for the event were already underway, he added.

"We don't want to sit back and not do anything and have people lined up out the door from here for the next 3km trying to get fuel or something to eat."

The caravan park is set to be expanded from 25 unpowered sites to 100.

Present and future challenges

Kununurra Visitor Centre chief executive Vivienne McEvoy said she had been responding to enquiries about the eclipse for a decade.

She said both big groups and families had started planning their travels to see the eclipse "first, not last".

Vivienne McEvoy says the visitors' centre has been receiving enquiries about the eclipse for the past decade. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

"If they wait until they see it in Sydney, then photos and all the amazing stuff that happens around an eclipse have already been posted on social media," Ms McEvoy said.

While the visitor centre and local tourism businesses are thinking ahead, discussing how to secure affordable airfares and accommodation, they are struggling with the impact of the Middle East war and the uncertainty it creates for both the present and the future.

Purnululu National Park in the East Kimberley is one of WA's tourism hotspots. (Supplied: Gary Annett)

While Ms McEvoy said she could not predict what the cost of fuel would be in two years, plans were being established to keep visitors safe.

The WA government has set aside $24.6 million in this year's budget towards the 2028 eclipse.

Ms McEvoy said it was important to keep visitors safe in the beautiful but unforgiving Kimberley environment.

"It's about keeping people safe where they think they can travel down a little goat track in their two-wheel-drive vehicle," she said.

Beyond the eclipse

Shire of Wyndham-East Kimberley president David Menzel said he hoped the funds would provide long-term community benefits.

David Menzel hopes funding for the eclipse will bring long-term benefits. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

"We're hoping some of the spend on the infrastructure needs might have some useful life after the event," he said.

Mr Menzel said upgraded campgrounds and tourism facilities were needed in a region with all the cards to attract international tourism, and only needed the right marketing and infrastructure to support it.

But the clock is ticking.

"We've got one dry season to prepare for this influx of visitors," Mr Menzel said.

World.title: 'Survivors won': Good character references abolished for sexual offenders
World.content:
A survivor advocate behind the campaign calling for good character references to be abolished in sentencing perpetrators of sexual offences has described the NSW reform as "an absolute victory".

On Tuesday, the NSW government helped pass a scaled-back version of its reforms, removing good character as a mitigating factor for sexual offences.

NSW Premier Chris Minns had wanted to abolish the consideration of an offender's good character for all crimes.

Harrison James and Jarad Grice co-founded the #YourReferenceAintRelevant campaign, which aims to remove the provision of good character references when sentencing convicted paedophiles.

The men, who both endured child sexual abuse, wished to transform their pain into purpose.

"It's a history day for victims and survivors of sexual violence," Mr James said.

" Those survivors will no longer have to sit in court and hear the person who harmed them lauded as a good person. It's an absolute victory. "

Mr James and Jarad Grice co-founded the Your Reference Ain't Relevant campaign. (ABC News: Sam Foster)

Mr James alleged his abuse began when he was only 13 years old at the hands of his stepmother.

His stepmother fled the country in 2019 and has never been convicted.

He said the government's reforms were proof that the past four years of advocacy had been worthwhile.

" Survivors won. After all of that pain of telling our stories relentlessly, and all the political noise, survivors persevered. "

Amendments were 'safeguard provisions', says Greens

Labor had sought to abolish the use of such evidence in sentencing for all crimes, but in the upper house, the Greens and Coalition would only support doing so for sexual offences.

Concerns with a total abolition of character at sentencing had also been expressed by groups such as Legal Aid NSW, the NSW Bar Association and the Law Society of NSW.

Multiple legal organisations disagreed with a total abolition of character at sentencing. (ABC News: Jak Rowland)

Some argued that recognising good character could encourage an offender to maintain or return to lawful behaviour, aligning with the justice system's core purpose of rehabilitation.

Domestic Violence NSW had also raised caution with the potential impacts on victim-survivors who were mis-identified as the person using violence, saying that without safeguards to address this, there would be a risk of compounding existing inequalities in the justice system.

Do you know more? If you have any information about the story, contact Isabella Ross.

NSW Attorney-General Michael Daley said those who had collaborated on the bill had expertise across academia, the justice system, criminal law and matters associated with victims of crime.

In a statement, Greens MP Sue Higginson acknowledged the "nation-leading reforms" but said "safeguard provisions" were necessary.

"Our amendments give courts the power to disregard character evidence for the most serious criminals," she said.

"The opposition and crossbench have ensured that vulnerable people can still put forward evidence of their good character for other offences to avoid harsher sentences.

" Sentencing is a complex process that must be left up to judges, not politicians. "

Sue Higginson says "safeguard provisions" were necessary for the bill. (AAP: Bianca de Marchi)

'Profoundly important moment for victims'

The NSW government said while the amendments gutted their bill, they would not stand in the way of change for sexual assault survivors.

Mr Minns said he was determined to extend the reform to all other offences and would introduce a separate bill on Wednesday.

Mr Daley said: "This is a critical reform for victim-survivors."

Mr James thanked Mr Minns for being "incredibly supportive" during campaigning for the NSW reform.

" He understands how difficult it is for someone like me to speak up about my experiences. "

Premier Chris Minns with Mr James, Mr Grice and Attorney-General Michael Daley. (Supplied)

Mr James said he felt disappointed with the Coalition and the Greens' stance, saying he did not want his story to be used as a "political football".

"I'm disappointed that the amendments didn't encapsulate crime types like domestic violence, homicide — very serious, violent offences," he said.

"But I think about what has been achieved, and that is a profoundly important moment for victims and survivors of sexual violence."

As for what the future now holds, Mr James said he would continue advocating for law changes to be implemented in jurisdictions across the country.

He said the younger version of himself "wouldn't believe" what he had overcome and achieved.

"I think if there was someone like me advocating when I was a 13, 14 and 15-year-old boy being sexually abused, I think it would have given me an immense sense of hope and determination that I can speak out.

"It sends a very clear message that this is a cultural shift as much as it is a legal one."

World.title: Eurovision pays musical homage to Austria-Australia confusion
World.content:
With blasts of dry ice and jets of flame, the Eurovision party kicked off inside the Wiener Stadthalle in Vienna, where more than 11,000 revved-up fans watched 15 countries battle for their place in the upcoming grand final on Saturday.

The contest, traditionally a celebration of pop music and high camp, has been mired in controversy over Israel's participation.

Despite significant boycotts, the broadcast went ahead on Tuesday night, local time, where 10 countries made it through to the next round.

Bzikebi from Georgia performs during the first semifinal of the 70th Eurovision Song Contest. (AP: Martin Meissner)

The results were determined through a mix of jury and public voting, from audiences all over the world, with a 50 per cent weighting given to each.

The 10 countries to qualify are:

Eurovision begins amid boycotts and massive police operation in Vienna But behind the colour and campness, this year's Eurovision Song Contest is shaping up to be among the most politically charged in history.

Belgium: Dancing on the Ice

Croatia: Andromeda

Finland: Liekinheitin

Greece: Ferto

Israel: Michelle

Lithuania: Solo quiero mas

Moldova: Viva, Moldova!

Poland: Pray

Serbia: Kraj mene

Sweden: My System

It was the end of the road for Portugal, Georgia, Montenegro, Estonia and San Marino.

The performances ranged from upbeat Estonian guitar pop to soaring Polish high notes, and the brooding mystery of Lithuania's silver-painted Lion Ceccah.

Moldova opened the show with rapper Satoshi pumping up the energy, before Serbian progressive metal band Lavina closed the evening with throat-shredding growl.

A member of Lavina, representing Serbia, performs Kraj Mene in Vienna, Austria. (Reuters: Lisa Leutner)

Fifteen more countries, including Australia, will compete in Thursday's second semifinal, with another 10 going through to Saturday's final in Vienna.

Britain, France, Germany and Italy have already guaranteed spots in the 25-country final, alongside hosts Austria.

Lion Ceccah, representing Lithuania, performs Solo Quiero Mas. (Reuters: Lisa Leutner)

No kangaroos in Austria

Australian singer Go-Jo, whose song Milkshake Man was the 2025 Eurovision entry, made a guest appearance at the event.

Joining Austrian hosts Victoria Swarovski and Michael Ostrowski, Go-Jo explained: "I was actually supposed to go home to Australia, but instead I landed in Austria because some idiot confused Australia with Austria," he said.

Go-Jo, who represented Australia at the 2025 Eurovision Song Contest, performed with Austria's Victoria Swarovski and Michael Ostrowski. (Reuters: Lisa Leutner)

Swarovski declared "Let's clear this once and for all. What's Austrian and what's Australian" before the trio broke into song.

Quips between the two nations were shared, declaring they are "opposites".

"Spiders, snakes and shark attacks, Australia would kill me."

'Your desserts, they cause heart attacks, and winter sports don't thrill me."

The trio performed the light-hearted interlude while they waited for the voting results. (AP: Martin Meissner)

The song and dance, accompanied by a kangaroo, culminated in a call and response from the crowd.

"I say kanga, you say roo!"

Australia's participation in the competition will kick off on Thursday in the second semifinal with Delta Goodrem's Eclipse.

Countries boycott Israel's participation

This year marks the 70th edition of Eurovision, which, despite its razzle dazzle, rarely escapes the geo-politics in the background.

National broadcasters in Spain, the Netherlands, Ireland, Slovenia and Iceland are boycotting the event, taking a stand over the war in Gaza, making this year the smallest Eurovision event since 2003, with just 35 entries.

Demonstrators set white paper boxes to look like children's coffins to protest against Israel ahead of the first semifinal in Vienna. (AP Photo: Martin Meissner)

The move will most likely reduce viewership from last year's estimated 166 million.

Tension in the city was palpable as protesters placed coffins in central Vienna, while inside the concert hall Israel's Noam Bettan performed pop song Michelle.

Noam Bettan from Israel reacts to the vote totals being announced. (AP: Martin Meissner)

Israel was among the 10 entries that received enough points from national juries and a public vote on Tuesday to qualify for the final on Saturday.

Reuters / AFP

World.title: New search for SA mother missing from outback opal town
World.content:
SA Police have returned to the outback town of Andamooka to search for missing local woman Trisha Graf.

Ms Graf, 41, was last seen driving in the town, about 600 kilometres north of Adelaide, in the early hours of December 12 last year.

The next day, her car was found abandoned near Blue Dam, about 4 kilometres east of Andamooka.

Police say investigators will search for evidence on the western fringe of Andamooka "over the next few days".

Police have conducted several searches over the past five months looking for the mother-of-two.

Police search mine shafts and disused opal diggings in March. (Supplied: SA Police)

Most recently, in March, they seized a car and searched locations including mine shafts and disused opal diggings.

Police say Ms Graf went to the Roxby Downs Hotel with a friend on the night of December 11 and was last seen there at 12:19am.

The pair then drove back to Andamooka, hitting a kangaroo on the way but continuing to the smaller town.

Ms Graf left her friend's house just before 2am and was last seen driving along Dunstan Drive, in Andamooka.

Ms Graf's partner and a friend found her car immobilised on a mound near Blue Dam about midday on December 12.

Trisha Graf's car, which was located damaged from a collision with a kangaroo and immobilised on a mound at Blue Dam. (ABC News: Carl Saville)

Her disappearance was declared a major crime on January 6.

Police have asked anyone with information about Ms Graf's whereabouts or her movements leading up to her disappearance to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000 or online at www.crimestopperssa.com.au.

World.title: Coronial inquest into death of tasered 95yo Clare Nowland begins
World.content:
A coronial inquest into the death of Clare Nowland is underway three years after the 95-year-old was tasered by a serving NSW Police officer in her Snowy Mountains aged care home.

The great-grandmother was a resident at Cooma's Yallambee Lodge in May 2023, when a staff member called Triple Zero (000) to report that she was wandering the property and entering other residents' rooms.

Paramedics and two police officers, including former senior constable Kristian White, found Ms Nowland a room, holding a steak knife against her walker.

CCTV footage captured Clare Nowland walking around the facility before she was tasered. (Supplied)

Within three minutes, White drew his taser, said "nah, bugger it" and discharged the weapon at the great-grandmother.

Ms Nowland fell, hit her head and died in hospital one week later after suffering an inoperable brain bleed.

At the time she weighed 47.5 kilograms and had symptoms consistent with dementia.

Kristian White was found guilty of manslaughter in 2024. (ABC News: Keana Naughton)

White was found guilty of manslaughter following a jury trial in the NSW Supreme Court in November 2024.

He avoided jail time over the death and was instead sentenced to a two-year community correction order and required to do 425 hours of community service.

At the time, Justice Ian Harrison said White's crime fell on the lower end of objective seriousness and was not premeditated.

He also noted that White showed remorse.

A subsequent appeal by Crown prosecutors to review that sentence was dismissed.

Clare Nowland was a resident at the Yallambee Lodge aged care facility in Cooma. (Four Corners: Sissy Reyes)

Coronial inquest opens

A three-day inquest looking into Ms Nowland's death has begun in the Queanbeyan Coroners Court in southern NSW.

Coronial inquests are designed to look at the manner and cause of a death, and to make recommendations to improve public safety.

In this case, the facts regarding the cause of death are not in dispute.

The inquest will be held in the Queanbeyan Courthouse over the next three days. (ABC South East NSW: Isla Evans)

Kristian White's actions on the night of May 17, 2023 — when he deployed the taser on Ms Nowland — were found to be excessive and not reasonably necessary.

White was removed from the NSW Police Force after the trial in 2024.

Focus on dementia training

The inquest is expected to focus on the guidelines and training given to aged-care staff, police and emergency services in dealing with people experiencing dementia.

It is also set to look at the way those people communicate with patients and how they de-escalate situations.

Witnesses representing police, ambulance and dementia training and advocacy groups are expected to give evidence.

Representatives for the Nowland family, the local Snowy Monaro Regional Council and the aged care provider are also expected to take part.

Clare Nowland's family wants the inquest to lead to change. (Supplied)

Ms Nowland's eldest son, Mike Nowland, previously spoke to the ABC's Four Corners program about the family's concerns about gaps in police training and policies around taser use, and said he hoped the inquest would lead to change.

The inquest before Coroner Teresa O'Sullivan is expected to continue until Friday.

World.title: 'Absolutely thrilled': Canberra's RSPCA to get new facility out of federal budget
World.content:
The RSPCA has welcomed a $30 million investment in a new purpose-built clinic at Pialligo in Tuesday night's federal budget.

The cash injection will go towards replacing the animal welfare organisation's more than 40-year-old centre at Weston.

"We are so, so pleased with the funding," RSPCA ACT chief executive Michelle Robertson said on ABC Radio Canberra this morning.

" This is absolutely a once in a generation opportunity for animal welfare so we are so, so, so happy. "

Federal budget 2026: Stay up to date with the budget aftermath in our live blog.

Other funding boosts for the ACT revealed in the budget papers include $50 million to duplicate Drake Brockman Drive in West Belconnen, aimed at servicing the area's growing population.

And Canberra's cultural institutions are set to benefit too, with almost $10 million over three years committed to the National Film and Sound Archive.

$4 million will be given towards developing the Ngurra Cultural Precinct on the Acton Peninsula, and the Museum of Australian Democracy will get $3 million to help mark the centenary of Old Parliament House.

Almost $10 million over three years has been allocated to the National Film and Sound Archive. (ABC News: Matthew Doran)

RSPCA 'absolutely thrilled'

RSPCA ACT has long called for support to build a new facility in Pialligo to improve animal welfare in the capital, and Ms Robertson said the promised $30 million will go a long way towards achieving that.

The ACT government also previously committed $2 million to the organisation in the 2025–26 budget.

"Combined with the ACT government commitment, which we've spoken about a number of times in the past, this enables us to build a new animal welfare campus and everything else that's required," Ms Robertson said.

"Construction is really expensive and there's a lot of additional enabling works ... that [need] to take place.

" But the long and short of it is, it's going to give us the opportunity to do the things that we really need to do, including having a purpose-built vet clinic so we can do high-volume desexing. "

She said they were "absolutely thrilled" because it would enable them the security to "do what need to do".

She said she was looking forward to getting started as soon as possible.

"We'd need to do a bit of community fundraising and capital fundraising as well, but hopefully as soon as possible, so we can get this done and we can do better for the animals and their humans in the ACT," she said.

'These are practical investments': Steel

The biggest budget commitment for Canberra announced last night is $50 million to duplicate Drake Brockman Drive in West Belconnen.

Other boosts in the budget papers include more than $2 million for the ACT to improve the health of the upper Murrumbidgee River, while an extra $1.4 million will go towards improving access to local youth mental health services.

More than $2 million has been allocated to improve the health of the upper Murrumbidgee River, pictured here at Tharwa. (Supplied: Andy Lowes)

Another $3 million will be invested over four years for the National Jewish Memorial Centre as part of the government's response to the Bondi Terror Attack.

And $200,000 has been committed to a victim-survivor support scheme.

ACT Treasurer Chris Steel said these investments, along with the $50 million in funding to improve the Canberra to Sydney rail line announced earlier this week, all showed a commitment to the city and its region.

"These are practical investments — that support jobs, connectivity, productivity and quality of life," he said.

" They reflect the reality that Canberra's infrastructure has to work harder because Canberra does more. "

$3 million was allocated to the Museum of Australian Democracy to help mark the centenary of Old Parliament House. (Gabrielle Rumble)

Mr Steel said the federal budget represented a "decisive shift toward fairer treatment of Canberra" and noted particularly the Commonwealth's investment of an additional $2 billion in the Housing Support Program, which the ACT can access.

"Housing remains the most pressing intergenerational issue facing Canberra, particularly for younger people, families and essential workers," he said.

" This budget recognises that housing supply must be treated as a national responsibility if we want fairness between generations. "

Mr Steel said the ACT government was "well positioned" to meet the funding requirements to "build more well-located homes sooner".

"Access to $50 million in funding will help to deliver more homes, as the ACT continues to lead the nation in delivering the National Housing Accord," he said.

ACT Treasurer Chris Steel said the federal budget represented a "decisive shift" towards investing in the territory. (ABC News: Toby Hunt)

'Important things' missing out: Pocock

But ACT independent Senator David Pocock was less effusive, describing the budget as a "real mixed bag".

"You've got to give them credit on the capital gains tax and negative gearing changes and then also dealing with trusts," Mr Pocock said.

"This is long overdue reform and I think finally as a country we're starting to say that housing should be more of a human right, something that's accessible and affordable rather than this asset class, this wealth creation vehicle that's part of the reason why we've landed in this housing crisis.

" I really commend the Treasurer on that. "

However, he said there were some missed opportunities otherwise.

From an ACT perspective, Mr Pocock said the infrastructure investment was "disappointing".

ACT Senator David Pocock described the federal budget as a "mixed bag". (ABC News: Luke Stephenson)

"If you look at it, I think we've just over $100 million out of a $9 billion new spend on infrastructure investment, and the headline one is $50 million to knock 15 minutes of travel time off Canberra to Sydney rail over five years," he said.

"That seems … fairly small, if you look at what's being thrown into the suburban rail loop in Melbourne, other infrastructure projects.

"So these things actually matter and are really important, not just for Canberrans, people in Sydney, but for our country."

He said there were also other major projects in the ACT that were still waiting on significant funding.

"Part of the problem is that the ACT government has no plans for those big things that we know we've needed for a very long time," he said.

"[The] Convention Centre, Stadium, they're still planning, despite for two decades knowing that the end of life is imminent for those facilities."

World.title: Australia axes quick as Women's T20 World Cup squad is named
World.content:
Brisbane Heat left-arm pace bowler Lucy Hamilton has been selected in Australia's T20 World Cup squad, with the experienced Darcie Brown a surprise omission.

Hamilton, who turned 20 earlier this month, will play in her first World Cup after making her international debut in all three formats in March.

Brown, who featured in Australia's T20 World Cup win in 2023, was not named in the 15-player squad on Wednesday ahead of this year's tournament, which will be hosted by England and Wales in June and July.

All-rounder Nicola Carey will play in her first T20 World Cup since 2020 after a golden summer which saw her return to the national side after a three-year absence.

The exclusion of right-arm quick Brown from the squad will be a major talking point.

"Darcie Brown was unlucky to miss out, but the decision was based on the conditions we're expecting and the makeup of the side," national team selector Shawn Flegler said.

"With at least six right-arm pace options in the mix and raw pace expected to be less effective, we opted to go with Lucy Hamilton, who offers something different as a left-arm quick."

Heat all-rounder Grace Harris returns to the side after being left out of the recent West Indies tour.

"She's a handy all-round option and someone who can take the game away from an opposition," Flegler said.

"We're pleased to welcome Annabel Sutherland back from an extended break as well. She's fresh and ready to go and will play an important role throughout the tournament."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Sophie Molineux will captain Australia for the first time at a World Cup in the wake of the recent retirement of legend Alyssa Healy.



"Sophie has already made her mark as captain and built a strong connection with the group over the last couple of tours, so we're looking forward to seeing what this side can achieve under her leadership," Flegler said.

"These squads are never easy to select but we're confident with the balance and stability we've got across the group. It's an experienced group and one we believe is capable of winning the World Cup."

New Zealand are the defending T20 world champions.

Australia will play three warm-up matches against South Africa, starting on May 31, with all games to be played at Arundel Castle.

Australia squad for Women's T20 World Cup

Sophie Molineux (captain), Ashleigh Gardner, Tahlia McGrath, Nicola Carey, Kim Garth, Lucy Hamilton, Grace Harris, Alana King, Phoebe Litchfield, Beth Mooney, Ellyse Perry, Megan Schutt, Annabel Sutherland, Georgia Voll, Georgia Wareham. Travelling reserve: Tahlia Wilson.

World.title: First openly gay NBA player Jason Collins dies at 47 of brain tumour
World.content:
Jason Collins, the NBA’s first openly gay player who went on to become a pioneer for inclusion and an ambassador for the league, has died from an aggressive form of a brain tumour, his family announced Tuesday.

Collins spent 13 years as a player in the league for six different franchises.

He revealed in 2013 that he was gay, an announcement that came toward the end of his playing career.

Collins had been diagnosed with Stage 4 glioblastoma, which has an extremely low survival rate. He was 47.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

“Jason changed lives in unexpected ways and was an inspiration to all who knew him and to those who admired him from afar," Collins' family said in a statement released through the NBA.

"We are grateful for the outpouring of love and prayers over the past eight months and for the exceptional medical care Jason received from his doctors and nurses. Our family will miss him dearly.”

Last week, Collins received the inaugural Bill Walton Global Champion Award at the Green Sports Alliance Summit. He was too ill to attend and his twin brother, former NBA player Jarron Collins, accepted the award on his behalf.

“I told my brother this before I came here: He’s the bravest, strongest man I’ve ever known,” Jarron Collins said.

Jason Collins averaged 3.6 points and 3.7 rebounds in his career. He helped the New Jersey Nets reach two NBA Finals and in his best season averaged 6.4 points and 6.1 rebounds for them in 2004-05.

World.title: The $67m Sydney university car park its own experts don’t want built
World.content:
NationalNSWCity life The $67m Sydney university car park its own experts don’t want built David Barwell May 13, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A car parking stoush is brewing at the University of NSW as a coalition of prominent academics moves to derail a $66.7 million expansion of a campus car park, warning the project risks locking in car dependence and undermining the institution’s climate goals. In a joint submission to the NSW Department of Planning, 12 professors and researchers across the university’s fields of transport, public health and law have urged the NSW government to reject the university’s proposal to add 505 new spaces at its Kensington campus. UNSW academics Dr Rona Macniven, Dr Chris Standen and Dr Hulya Gilbert, pictured at the carpark. Steven Siewert The plan would involve adding three levels to the existing Barker Street car park, which the university says is part of a broader effort to improve campus safety and “placemaking”. However, the submission warns the move will entrench a “status quo” of car culture and lead to “induced demand”, a well-established concept in which increasing parking capacity encourages more people to drive, leading to higher congestion and emissions.



“This proposal is completely misaligned with pretty much any university strategy you could name,” said the submission’s lead author Dr Christopher Standen, a research fellow at the university’s faculty of medicine and health, and school of building environment. “The university has a target of 85 per cent of students and staff travelling by sustainable modes. As far as records go back, they have consistently failed to meet that. Encouraging more people to drive isn’t going to help.” A concept image of the expanded carpark. University of NSW UNSW argues consolidating parking into one structure would allow future removal of central campus car parks to accommodate green space and new buildings. But the academics estimate the embodied carbon from construction alone would exceed 3 million kilograms of carbon dioxide equivalent — roughly comparable to 20 million kilometres of driving — before factoring in emissions from increased vehicle use. That, they argue, sits uneasily alongside UNSW’s 2030 net zero strategy.



Standen likened the proposal to motorway expansions, where adding lanes often produces only temporary relief before congestion returns. “It’s the same with parking supply,” he said. “If you increase the supply, the demand increases – especially when parking at the university costs as low as $8 a day, which inflates demand.” The proposed development is under assessement by the NSW Department of Planning. University of NSW The dispute reflects a broader divide in how institutions approach lower-carbon transport. While UNSW is pursuing expansion, other universities — including the University of Sydney and UTS — are planning growth without new multi-storey car parks. Governments are also limiting parking to encourage public transport use including Inner West Council which has proposed capping parking requirements in new housing developments.



The academics argue that, for a fraction of the cost, the university could fund a dedicated cycle path to nearby Green Square – where thousands of students live just four kilometres away – or provide public transport incentives for the 45,000 staff and students who attend the Kensington campus daily. Related Article City life More than 5000 rooms are planned in these Sydney suburbs. None will count as a home The submission also raises health concerns, including particulate pollution from tyre and brake wear, along with noise and air pollution it argues “disproportionately affects disadvantaged populations”. In a statement, a UNSW spokeswoman said the project would improve safety and accessibility, noting many commute from areas without easy public transport. The spokeswoman added that the university “supports academic freedom and respects the role of staff in contributing to public discussion.”



She said the project would also include sustainability measures including EV charging spaces, rooftop solar panels, and be designed as an all-electric building. For the dissenting academics, such measures do little to offset what they see as a fundamental contradiction. “As a leading global university, UNSW should be following best practice,” the submission stated. “Instead, we are entrenching the status quo.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Trump said Xi will give him ‘a big, fat hug’. This is what experts predict will really happen
World.content:
WorldAsiaChina relations Trump said Xi will give him ‘a big, fat hug’. This is what experts predict will really happen Lisa Visentin May 13, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Beijing: Ever his own hype man, US President Donald Trump set expectations high for the bonhomie he and Chinese leader Xi Jinping will project to the world when they meet in Beijing on Thursday. “President Xi will give me a big, fat hug when I get there in a few weeks,” Trump posted on Truth Social last month, claiming that China was “very happy that I am permanently opening the Strait of Hormuz”. Chinese leader Xi Jinping will host Donald Trump in Beijing this week, in the first state visit by a US leader in almost a decade. Matt Willis It’s part of Trump’s well-versed routine of promoting his friendship with – and at times fawning admiration for – Xi, which contrasts starkly with the tensions and suspicion between their two countries that span almost every policy area. Fast-forward one month, and it’s looking like a bold prediction by Trump, not just because Xi is hardly renowned for his public displays of affection, nor has he matched Trump’s effusiveness about their apparent friendship. But mostly because the Iran war is now dragging into its third month. The Strait is still closed, blockaded by both the US and Iran, with a ceasefire hanging by a thread.



Related Article Updated

Middle East at war ‘I don’t think about Americans’ financial situation’ in Iran war, Trump says as inflation bites Trump’s state visit to China – the first by an American president in almost a decade – was delayed in March to get clear air from the Iran war. But the issue looks set for a high billing on the summit agenda this week anyway, with Trump expected to press Xi on China’s relationship with Tehran and support for reopening the critical shipping lane during the two-day talks. It’s not clear how much this could reshape negotiations, but some analysts see it as strengthening China’s hand. “That will be something he really needs China’s help with because it looks like the bilateral negotiations between the United States and Iran are not going anywhere,” says Chucheng Feng, a Beijing-based founder of Hutong Research, a consultancy firm. “The US rare earths and critical mineral stockpile is also fast depleting. That also requires China’s supply. If you really think about it from a short-term perspective, China has the upper hand for sure.”



China analyst Arthur Kroeber, from research firm Gavekal Dragonomics, says the summit optics favour Xi. “Trump’s trade war is in disarray: most of his tariffs have been ruled illegal, and China’s exports continue to boom despite US protectionism. Trump’s war with Iran is also a mess,” he wrote in a recent analysis. For some time now, Washington and Beijing have signalled that stabilising the fragile detente in the US-China relationship is the key goal of this summit, lowering expectations of a major breakthrough on economic policy or anything else. Xi dines at Mar-a-Lago in April 2017. Trump later recounted how he informed the Chinese leader he had just launched air strikes on Syria while the pair enjoyed a “beautiful piece of chocolate cake” for dessert. AP Many analysts anticipate that the Beijing summit will achieve little beyond securing an extension of the trade truce that Xi and Trump sealed at their last meeting in Busan, South Korea, six months ago. And maybe lock in some extra purchase orders of US beef, soybeans and other exports.



This doesn’t scupper the significance of the summit. Trump may not get the bear hug he is looking for, but both men place a premium on leader-to-leader relations, meaning the rapport built on Xi’s turf will be critical in setting the stage for at least two other potential meetings between Trump and Xi this year. Related Article Opinion

Middle East at war ‘Eating bitterness’: China is set up to outlast Trump’s America This buys the Trump Administration more time to lock in “wins” on trade, while Xi can fine-tune his attempts to convince Trump to roll back support for Taiwan, both rhetorically and in its weapons sales to the democratic island. “The Taiwan question is not simply one issue among many, but the core of China’s core interests and the most sensitive red line in bilateral relations,” state media publication China Daily said in an editorial previewing the summit. Trump, on Monday (US time), said he planned to “have that discussion” with Xi about arms sales at the summit, though US officials have briefed reporters that there are no plans to change US policy on Taiwan.



“Put simply, Trump is not that bad for China. He is viewed as the dove on China policy in the White House,” says Zhao Minghao, an international relations expert at Shanghai’s Fudan University. Zhao reflects a common view among Chinese scholars that Beijing is increasingly confident it has the tools to weather, and even outmanoeuvre, the “Trump shock”, which quickly escalated into a triple-digit tariff war last year before China flexed its stranglehold over rare-earth metals. Concern grows over strait shutdown Since the war in Iran started in February, China experts have debated whether Beijing has any meaningful influence over Iran, its friend and economic partner, and, if so, what it would take for Xi to leverage that influence and what he might seek to extract in return. But there are signs, too, that China is growing increasingly concerned about the impasse in the Gulf, despite its considerable oil reserves. Its export-oriented economy hinges on open shipping lanes, and about half of its oil imports and almost one-third of its LNG imports transit through the Middle East.



It took two months, but in April, Xi made his first comments calling for the Strait to be opened – a position Foreign Minister Wang Yi repeated when he hosted his Iranian counterpart in Beijing last week. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi meets his Chinese counterpart, Wang Yi, in Beijing. AP “China has great reason to help mediate this conflict. The question is how to avoid the Iranian conflict becoming more and more negative in impacting US-China relations,” says Zhao. There is plenty of friction on this front going into the summit, and plenty of scepticism on the US side that Beijing actually wants to play a mediating role beyond offering ceasefire calls from the sidelines. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, a key architect of the summit on the American side, has called on China to “get the Iranians to open the strait”, while accusing Beijing of “funding the largest state sponsor of terrorism” by purchasing 90 per cent of Iran’s oil.



China, meanwhile, took the unprecedented step last week of ordering its refineries to ignore US sanctions on Iranian oil, signalling Beijing’s growing confidence to defy Washington’s pressure. Only days ago, the US state department sanctioned three Chinese companies it accused of “providing satellite imagery that enables Iran’s military strikes against US forces in the Middle East”. As former American ambassador to China Nicholas Burns put it recently, “no matter who’s in power in Washington and in Beijing in the future, I think we’re going to be stuck with this highly competitive relationship for well more than a decade to come.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Spygate 2.0: The cheating saga which could blow up the Premier League promotion race
World.content:
SportSoccerEngland Spygate 2.0: The cheating saga which could blow up the Premier League promotion race Vince Rugari May 13, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Socceroos star Riley McGree’s bid to reach the English Premier League with Middlesbrough has fallen short in heartbreaking fashion. Again. Or has it? Socceroo Riley McGree (left) scored the opener on Wednesday morning. Getty Images English football is in unchartered territory after Southampton progressed to the Championship play-off final at Boro’s expense in a spiteful clash on Wednesday morning (AEST) – days after they were charged by the English Football League for spying on their opponents, which could lead to them being kicked out of the race for promotion, and the $370 million windfall that comes with it. Even though their season is now officially over, Boro is reportedly set to continue training in the hope that they could earn a last-minute reprieve from the EFL – which could, in turn, further delay McGree’s arrival to the Socceroos’ World Cup pre-camp in Florida.



Last week, two days before the first leg of the play-off semi-final, an analyst from Southampton was caught red-handed in the bushes at Middlesbrough’s headquarters, filming one of their training sessions. The analyst was reportedly confronted, deleted the footage he had captured and left the area, but it prompted an immediate investigation from the EFL, which has referred the case to an independent disciplinary commission. Southampton have been charged with breaking two EFL regulations which prohibit teams from observing an opponent’s training session within 72 hours of a match, and requires clubs to act with “utmost good faith” towards others. Kim Hellberg (Middlesbrough) and Tonda Eckert (Southampton) clash on the sidelines. Getty Images These rules were tightened after the first edition of ‘Spygate’ in 2019, when then-Leeds United boss Marcelo Bielsa admitted he had sent an assistant coach to watch Derby County train before a play-off match, revealing it was part of a systematic approach to gathering intel on rivals that he had deployed throughout his career. Back then, such activity was not strictly prohibited by the EFL, and so Leeds were punished only with a fine. But that moral grey area is now black and white, with sporting sanctions firmly on the table – including expulsion from the play-off final, in the most dramatic scenario – if Southampton are found guilty.



The problem is the independent commission has not yet made a ruling, and may not do so until the identity of the third and final team to clinch promotion to the Premier League is settled next weekend in the final at Wembley – popularly described as the “richest” game in English football because of the financial spoils that go to the victor. At this stage, it will involve Southampton and Hull City, but that could soon change, with the EFL having requested an expedited hearing. View post on X After a 0-0 draw in the first leg played at Middlesbrough’s Riverside Stadium, their manager Kim Hellberg said every club in the Championship should be “angry” about Southampton’s conduct; since then, rivals from other clubs in England’s second division have reportedly approached Boro with concerns that they, too, may have been subjected to Southampton’s prying eyes this season. The club, however, privately maintains that the analyst caught in the bushes was a “lone wolf”, and not part of a Bielsa-esque spying strategy, and has asked for more time to conduct an internal review.



“Some people say it doesn’t give you a big advantage. That’s wrong. It’s a massive advantage,” Hellberg said on the weekend. “Without it, it would have been impossible for them to know our shape in the first half. We have never used that shape before today … “Someone at Southampton has made the decision to go and cheat. That’s clear. It’s just wrong.” Southampton fans celebrate their victory - but their fate is in the hands of an independent disciplinary commission. Getty Images McGree, who turned down the chance to join Ange Postecoglou at Celtic to sign for Boro in 2022 and chase his Premier League dreams, scored the opening goal in Wednesday’s second leg after just five minutes – but Southampton equalised on the stroke of half-time, held on to force the tie to go into extra time, then scored the winning goal in the 116th minute through Shea Charles to seal a 2-1 aggregate victory. Speaking afterwards, a shattered Hellberg paid tribute to Southampton’s players and fans – but notably, not their coaching staff – and insisted a fine would not be adequate punishment.



Southampton coach Tonda Eckert. Getty Images “If we didn’t catch that man who they sent up, five hours to drive, you would sit here and say ‘well done’ maybe in the tactical aspects of the game, and I would go home and feel like I have failed in that aspect that I had to help my players,” Hellberg said. Related Article Analysis

Premier League Game of throw-ins: Has the Premier League become too obsessed with control? “But when that is taken away from you, when someone decides: ‘Nah, we’re not going to watch every game, we’ll send someone instead, we’ll film the session, and see everything, and hope they don’t get caught’ … it breaks my heart.” Asked if he had spoken to his counterpart, Southampton manager Tonda Eckert, Hellberg said: “No, I have nothing to say to him.”



Eckert was pressed on the spying allegations in his own post-match press conference. He initially offered a “no comment” but then, after being asked if he was a “cheat” with the second question, walked out – just as he did after repeated questioning after the first leg. What happens next is anyone’s guess. Football has a new Home. Stream the Premier League, UEFA Champions League, Emirates FA Cup, UEFA Europa League and more live & on demand on Stan Sport.

World.title: ASX lower, CBA plunges as bank stocks fall; Healius plummets
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX lower, CBA plunges as bank stocks fall; Healius plummets Staff writers Updated May 13, 2026 — 11:24am ,first published May 13, 2026 — 5:21am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket opened lower for the fourth day in a row, as the Middle East war drags on without resolution in sight and financial stocks slumped with CBA, the nation’s biggest bank, plunging after it reported lower-than-expected quarterly profits. The S&P/ASX 200 was down 41.40 points, or 0.5 per cent, at 8629.30 shortly after 11am AEST, weighed down by the banks and by tech stocks, which were in the red after a screeching halt in their US rally put the brakes on Wall Street’s record-setting run. The ASX lost 0.4 per cent on Tuesday. Local investors were also digesting the ramifications of the federal budget, which was delivered on Tuesday night. The Australian dollar was trading at US72.36¢ in late morning. Wall Street retreated from its record highs. AP Banking stocks led the early declines, with the Commonwealth Bank plummeting 8.3 per cent after its quarterly profits missed market expectations, while the wider banking sector also fell sharply amid warnings of weaker housing credit growth due to the federal budget’s measures on housing. Westpac was down 2.8 per cent, while National Australia Bank lost 2.3 per cent and ANZ Bank fell 1.7 per cent. Financial stocks make up about a third of the ASX.



CBA reported $2.7 billion in third-quarter profits, which was 4 per cent higher than a year earlier, but below market predictions. The numbers came as analysts warned the budget’s policies on housing investment would weigh on lending growth and dampen sentiment towards housing - the largest source of loans for Australian banks. CBA and Westpac are the biggest mortgage lenders. Citi analyst Thomas Strong said CBA’s profit was slightly below expectations, as was its capital (a buffer held by banks for protecting them against financial shocks). CBA had raised its provisions for bad debts, adding $200 million, in response to growing economic risks from rising inflation and the war in the Middle East. Related Article Analysis

Federal budget Revealed: The winners and losers from the 2026 federal budget “Coupled with the likely negative sentiment towards housing and credit growth out of the Federal Budget delivered overnight, we expect the result could be negatively received,” Strong said. Macquarie analysts said the budget’s changes were likely to result in “slower house price and credit growth, which could weigh on bank earnings and share prices.”



Tech stocks were the other big weight on the ASX. A selloff in high-flying chipmakers drove US stocks lower overnight, with the market also falling alongside bonds after US inflation data showed the impacts of energy disruptions on the world’s largest economy stemming from the war in Iran. WiseTech Global shares fell 4 per cent, pushing the software maker’s market value below that of Xero, which slipped 0.2 per cent and is now Australia’s biggest tech stock. Technology One shares dropped 1.1 per cent and data centre operator Next DC fell 0.9 per cent. Healius shares plummeted 20.6 per cent after the pathology services provider lowered its full-year profit forecasts and flagged the sale of its Agilex Biolabs business, citing a fall in GP attendances over the past months and softer pathology volumes, while costs continued to rise. The company warned that as last night’s budget included no new funding for pathology services, “charging out-of-pocket fees for pathology tests is the only viable option left to bridge the funding gap.” Blunting the losses on the ASX were gains again by the mining heavyweights. BHP climbed another 2.1 per cent on its record close last night, while rivals Rio Tinto and Fortescue Metals rose 1.8 per cent and 0.7 per cent. Gold miners Northern Star Resources (up 1.3 per cent) and Evolution Mining (up 1.7 per cent) also advanced. Prices for copper, BHP’s future key metal as it’s pivoting away from iron ore, jumped above $US14,000 a tonne to a record high overnight as a rebound in Chinese demand and mounting supply risks outweigh concerns about the Iran war’s impact on global growth. BHP this morning also announced that former BlueScope Steel CEO Mark Vassella will join its board as non-executive director next month.



Energy stocks were little changed, with Woodside up 0.2 per cent and Santos up 0.8 per cent. Oil prices steadied overnight, having gained almost 8 per cent over the past three sessions as a resolution to the Middle East conflict remains elusive, with Iranian exports showing further strain from a US Naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude traded near $US107 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate futures were below $US102. On Wall Street overnight, the S&P 500 fell 0.2 per cent from its all-time high set the day before. The Dow Jones added 56 points, or 0.1 per cent, while the Nasdaq composite sank 0.7 per cent from its own record. Related Article Opinion

Middle East at war ‘Eating bitterness’: China is set up to outlast Trump’s America Some of the sharpest drops hit chip companies and stocks that had been on electric runs because of the artificial-intelligence boom. Intel slumped 6.8 per cent after its stock had more than tripled so far this year. Micron Technology dropped 3.6 per cent after coming into the day with a gain of nearly 180 per cent for the year to date, and CoreWeave sank 6.1 per cent to cut into its gain of 60 per cent for 2026. The pullback for AI stocks began earlier in the day in Asia, where South Korea’s Kospi index sank 2.3 per cent from its all-time high on worries that the government may redistribute windfall AI profits from companies to its citizens.



Also weighing on Wall Street were oil prices as the war with Iran threatens to drag on. The resulting leap for crude oil prices, with Brent up from roughly $US70 per barrel before the war, caused inflation in the United States to worsen last month by more than economists expected, according to a report released overnight. In another discouraging signal, price increases accelerated by more in April than economists expected even after excluding petrol and food costs. That could be a result of tariffs and bad weather also pushing prices higher, according to Brian Jacobsen, chief economic strategist at Annex Wealth Management. Treasury yields rose in the bond market following an initial zigzag, suggesting traders suspect the Federal Reserve will keep interest rates high to combat inflation. The Fed has been keeping its cuts to interest rates on hold recently, as it waits to see how high inflation will go because of the war with Iran and the tariffs introduced by Trump. That’s because lower rates can worsen inflation at the same time that they give the economy a boost. The yield on the 10-year Treasury rose to 4.45 per cent from 4.42 per cent late on Monday and remains well above its 3.97 per cent level from before the war.



Related Article Opinion

Trade wars Trump’s ‘Hail Mary’ attempt to save his war on the world Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist GameStop fell 3.5 per cent after eBay rejected a buyout offer from the much smaller company, calling it “neither credible nor attractive.” It highlighted uncertainty about how GameStop would raise the money to pay for the purchase, among other challenges for the deal, and eBay’s stock rose 2.1 per cent. In other international markets, indexes mostly fell across Europe and Asia. Besides South Korea’s tumble, losses of 1.6 per cent for Germany’s DAX and 0.9 per cent for France’s CAC 40 were some of the world’s sharpest.
